analysis.one_liner: Blocks a safety rule that would give truck drivers more rest by limiting their hours of service.
analysis.headline: The bill to block the truck driver rest rule never left committee: no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2000, the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration proposed a rule rewriting how many hours truck drivers may work before resting, aimed at reducing crashes caused by fatigue. This bill would have forbidden the Transportation Secretary and the FMCSA from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing that rule, and from spending any federal money on it. It would have let the agency keep working on the rule behind the scenes, but any final rule could not take effect until 180 days after being sent to Congress. The bill was introduced by Sen. James Inhofe and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, motor carriers — the trucking companies — would benefit most, because they could keep drivers on duty under the old, longer hours without paying for more drivers or reworking schedules. Shippers relying on long-haul trucking would also avoid any rate increases tied to shorter driver hours.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the Transportation Secretary and FMCSA Administrator from taking any action or spending appropriated funds to finalize, implement, or enforce the proposed 'Hours of Service of Drivers; Driver Rest and Sleep for Safe Operations' rule published May 2, 2000.

It would allow the agency to continue all earlier stages of rulemaking — including a supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking — but bar adoption of a final rule, and delay any final rule's effective date until 180 days after it is transmitted to Congress.

analysis.who_pays: Truck drivers, who would keep working shifts under the old hours-of-service limits with less mandated rest, and everyone sharing the road with trucks, since fatigued driving is a known crash risk the proposed rule targeted. Safety advocates' multi-year effort to modernize the rules would also be nullified by statute.
analysis.who_pays_short: Truck drivers and everyone on the road

drawbacks.text: The bill would override an agency safety rulemaking by statute, preventing regulators from addressing driver fatigue — the stated target of the 'Driver Rest and Sleep for Safe Operations' rule.

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill was cost: the 2000 proposal's restrictions on driver scheduling would reduce fleet productivity, force carriers to hire more drivers, and raise shipping costs, and carriers argued its one-size-fits-all rest cycle did not match how drivers actually sleep.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered savings for carriers and shippers but its core effect was to block, by statute, a safety rule aimed at crashes caused by tired drivers. The costs would fall on truck drivers' rest and on public safety, and the bill offered no substitute safety measure — it was a stoppage, not a rewrite, which is why even one cosponsor did not sign on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, got no hearing or vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. James Inhofe introduced S. 614 on March 26, 2001.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day; the action history shows no further action of any kind.
The bill never advanced and expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Truck drivers and everyone who shares the road with trucks came out ahead, because the statute blocking the fatigue-safety rulemaking never passed. Trucking carriers also gained in the near term, since the restrictions never took effect during that Congress.

for.name: Sen. James Inhofe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to block the hours-of-service rule from being finalized or enforced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have spared carriers the cost of the proposed rule, which limited how long drivers could stay on duty. The savings come at the public's expense: fatigued drivers are a crash risk the rule was written to address.
The bill would have kept the old, longer hours-of-service limits, so drivers would get less mandated rest. Their interest in more rest runs alongside public safety.
